This book argues that such a foundation exists, and that it is revealed in the most elemental feature of lived experience, which is the ability to direct one’s own focus. Before intention or choice, before deliberation or desire, there is the self-evident act of orienting awareness, and from this act emerges a new first principle articulated in the axiom Focō, ergo volō, \\\"I focus therefore I will\\\". This axiom is not a metaphysical posit and it is not an empirical conjecture. It stands in the transcendental register where its truth is demonstrated in the very effort to examine or deny it, for any attempt to assess the claim already performs the act it identifies. The capacity to locate, shift or withhold attention is the primordial gesture through which an agent discloses itself as the source of its own activity. A Defense of Focō, ergo volō establishes the philosophical legitimacy of this axiom and justifies its place as the irreducible ground upon which all accounts of agency must rest. Descartes’ Cogito secured the certainty of the thinking self. This work explicates the originary activity through which that self becomes capable of authorship. Can automated provers avoid mistakes (as well as experiences and prejudices) to provide objective verification? And can an automated prover's claims be provably verified? We will follow examples of proofs that were found to be flawed, but then corrected (as the proof plan was sufficiently robust), as well as accepted \\\"proofs\\\" that turned out to be fundamentally wrong.
